analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for discount retailers to sue manufacturers who cut them off for selling too cheaply.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 235-157, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responded to Supreme Court decisions that made it very hard for a discount store to prove a manufacturer was punishing it for cutting prices. It would let a reseller win a price-fixing case by showing that a competitor complained about its prices and the manufacturer then cut it off, and it would make any deal between a maker and a seller to set or maintain resale prices automatically illegal. It passed the House in April 1990 but the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, consumers would gain from more price competition: discount stores, drugstores, and other resellers could keep discounting without fear of being cut off by brand-name suppliers, and courts would no longer throw out their cases on technical evidence grounds.

how_it_helps.text: A reseller could win a price-fixing case simply by showing a competitor complained about its prices and the manufacturer then terminated it as a dealer or refused to supply it.
An agreement between a manufacturer and a reseller to set, change, or maintain resale prices would itself be a violation, even if no specific price level was agreed on.
An agreement to cut off another dealer because of that dealer's pricing policies would be a violation whether or not a specific price was agreed to.
The bill preserved the ordinary antitrust review for territorial and location restraints, limiting its reach to price-related agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name manufacturers and their suppliers would bear the cost: easier lawsuits, automatic illegality for resale price deals, and retroactive exposure for suits already filed when the bill passed the House.

drawbacks.text: By making any agreement to set or maintain resale prices automatically illegal, the bill could also sweep in efficient distribution arrangements and expose manufacturers to lawsuits even where the restraint had little effect on consumers.
The version passed by the House applied the new price-agreement rules to lawsuits already pending, giving manufacturers retroactive liability in existing cases.

Manufacturers argued that relaxed rules would chill legitimate supplier decisions to choose their dealers, though courts would still have been able to reject a case if no reasonable inference of concerted action could be drawn.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed at a real consumer problem: when suppliers punish discounters, shoppers pay more. The main cost falls on manufacturers in the form of easier and potentially retroactive lawsuits, and the strongest objection is that the bright-line rule could catch some pro-competitive distribution deals. The bill tried to limit that by keeping normal antitrust review for territorial restraints, but it remains a broad rule drawn to favor plaintiffs.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 235-157, the Senate put it on its calendar in May 1990, and no senator ever voted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 1989 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which reported it with a written report in March 1990.
The House passed it on April 18, 1990 by a recorded vote of 235 to 157, after a motion to recommit failed on a voice vote.
The vote split sharply by party: 212 of 257 House Democrats voted yes while only 23 of 175 House Republicans did.
The Senate received the bill on April 19, 1990, its Judiciary Committee was discharged by unanimous consent, and the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar on May 17, 1990.
The bill never received a Senate vote and died when that Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name manufacturers that enforce resale prices came out ahead, because the bill that would have exposed them to easier price-fixing lawsuits never became law. Discount retailers and their customers did not get the new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name manufacturers that set resale prices

for.name: Rep. Jack Brooks
for.role: House Judiciary Committee Chairman and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through the House Judiciary Committee to passage.

for.name: 15 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support in the House.

for.name: Discount retailers and consumer groups
for.what_they_did: Backed the bill as a way to protect discounting from supplier retaliation.

against.name: 134 of 175 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 23 voting yes and 134 voting no.

against.name: Senate majority leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a Senate vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar in May 1990, and it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Brand-name manufacturer trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would make legitimate supplier-dealer agreements subject to automatic antitrust liability.

against.name: Rep. Hamilton Fish
against.role: House Republican on the Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to committee on the House floor; the motion failed on a voice vote.

sides.party_line_note: House passage was 235-157, but the split was stark: 212 of 257 Democrats voted yes (82%) while only 23 of 175 Republicans did (13%).

industries.note: The bill made their agreements with dealers over resale prices automatically illegal and let terminated discounters prove conspiracy with a simple showing, exposing them to easier lawsuits, including retroactively. Their ability to enforce uniform retail prices depends on discounters being unable to win such suits.

Discounters would gain legal protection: a supplier that cut them off after a competitor complained about their prices could be sued successfully. That aligns with consumers' interest in lower prices.
